toc.title: Respect what it has been doing
The ideal: notice it and hold back
Two extremes, and a lot of room in between
A middle step: permission, with a condition

blocks.p: Do you use negative coping skills to reduce your numbness, your panic, your feelings of being alone, or maybe rage or something else? You're absolutely not alone. I think a lot of people do. Those emotions are really challenging, to say the least. Here's a framework for understanding those negative coping skills and slowly stopping them, so that you can relieve your shame and your judgment.

blocks.h: Respect what it has been doing

blocks.p: I call these coping skills behavioral adaptations. If they're destructive, don't do them. If it's cutting, I don't want people to do that.

I work with people who struggle with something like "I want to eat to feel better." Okay, let's just respect that. That's a way your body has come up with, and it has been successful in a way. It has successfully contained your defensive activation and made you feel better. So in a way, it has worked. Let's respect it for what it is.
But what I'm hearing is that you want to do something different. Great. That's fantastic. It's really hard to stop, but I recognize you want to stop.

blocks.h: The ideal: notice it and hold back

blocks.p: The ideal is that you notice the activation and pull back on the behavioral adaptation. Maybe you give yourself a little bit of time to feel it, and then allow another thought to pop into your mind, or go to your safety anchoring menu, or whatever it is. That would be fantastic.
But that is very, very difficult. So think of what follows as a framework: steps toward that ideal.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Two extremes, and a lot of room in between

blocks.p: One extreme is an F-it attitude. Someone is in dysregulation, and they've reached maybe fight, or rage: F it. That's the extreme of behavioral adaptation.

The other extreme is depriving yourself completely, even of something you genuinely enjoy. Maybe I like Oreos a lot. (I'm just saying Oreos as an example. I have no idea if that's anybody's go-to or not.) The extreme would be: I can't have access to this. You don't have it in the home, so it's not even an option. Maybe that's real. Maybe that's what someone needs.
In between those extremes, I think there are a lot of options:

ul: I caught it, and I did something else. Great job. Pat yourself on the back.
F it, I'm going to do it, but I'll restrict myself to five Oreos instead of ten.
F it, but here's my constraint: I'm going to eat my five Oreos, and then I'm going to scream.
F it, I'm going to eat as many Oreos as I want, but I have to take one deep breath between each one.

blocks.p: None of these is going to be pleasurable. I'm not saying that whatsoever. The question is how we go from the extreme toward mindfulness. How can we work our way back toward mindfulness?

blocks.h: A middle step: permission, with a condition

blocks.p: Here's one intermediate step. The next time you notice yourself going toward the Oreos, or the ice cream, or whatever it is, catch it and tell yourself:

"I'm allowed to do this if I want to. I'm an adult. I can make that choice, and I'll give myself permission. But first I'm going to give myself five minutes. I'm going to take a deep breath in another room, or walk around the block, or do something else. And when I come back, if I still want it, I might give myself permission to have it."

At that point, it's just a choice you're making, without judgment. It might buy you a little bit of time. You're giving yourself permission, but you're also taking complete ownership over it. If you do choose it, that's just a choice you made, and there's no point in beating yourself up over it. We'll see what happens next time.
The contingency is that you have to do something to create time between realizing you're in the behavioral adaptation and acting on it.

So how do we make steps toward a goal like "I want to reduce my binge eating"? What's the step that's going to help you out this next time? Because it will come up again. Be honest with yourself about where you can notice it.

Maybe you won't be able to notice that you're in the behavioral adaptation until you're actually in it. You're not far enough along with your safety state development to recognize it before it's there.
Or maybe you're far enough along to recognize it before that first bite, but at that distance it's like, "I can't fight this." And maybe that's real.
Or maybe you're far enough along in developing your safety state that as you're walking toward the kitchen, you think, "Oh, I know what's happening. I see it unfolding before me."

Ideally, you notice it as some mild dysregulation, before the behavioral adaptation even kicks in. So the question is how we can break this process up to make it more likely that you'll do a safety anchoring exercise or an unstucking exercise instead.

All or nothing does not typically work for most people. If you can do it, go right ahead. But there might be a baby step you can make now. And then the next day: can I do one step better? Can I eat one Oreo less than yesterday? Can I take two deep breaths between each Oreo instead of one? Can we draw out the potential for more safety in our system, and less dysregulation?

Preparation is actually one of the stages of change. The first stage is not even being aware you need change. The second stage is contemplation. The third, I think, is preparation. That's where you know you have a problem, and you're not quite ready to do anything about it, but you're preparing for it. You're putting things into place.

Maybe one of those things is a final day: "I'm going to give myself two weeks to do my behavioral adaptation, but every day I'm going to do it less and less, and on this final day, I'm going to stop."

Preparation could also be: "I know I'm going to do this thing anyway. How can I minimize the impact I'm having on myself? What else can I set up?" Maybe a deep breath between bites. Maybe that's a regulation station, where you go and use your safety anchors, fidgets, or coping skills.

The ideal is that we can have food and be at peace with it: be in the moment, taste it, enjoy it, and maybe socialize. That's actually one end of the spectrum. The other end is complete dysregulation, where the behavioral adaptation takes over.
So how do you work toward the ideal? Maybe you'll never get there. That's not the point. The point is how you can work your way toward it, with more self-regulation involved.
